title: Judith (Judith 8–13)
hookLine: a widow rebukes the elders for testing God and saves her city

cards: A small hill town called Bethulia is under siege. The general Holofernes has surrounded it with a huge army and cut off the springs. The cisterns are running dry, and children are fainting in the streets.
The people shout at their leaders: surrender. Better slaves and alive than watch our children die of thirst. So the chief elder, Ozias, makes a deal.
Hold out five more days. If God hasn't helped us by then, we'll open the gates. It even sounds like faith.
And a widow in the town hears about it.

teach.b: Her name is Judith, which simply means a Jewish woman, a woman of Judea.
Her husband had died of sunstroke at the barley harvest, and for over three years she'd lived as a widow, fasting and praying, wealthy and respected; nobody, the book says, spoke an ill word of her.
She sends for the elders and doesn't soften it. Who are you to put God to the test?

teach.h: YOU SET A DEADLINE FOR GOD'S MERCY.
teach.b: You've set a deadline for the mercy of the Lord. God isn't a man, to be threatened or bargained with. If he wants to save us, he can, in his own time.
Then she tells them she has a plan, and not to ask what it is.
She prays, trades her widow's clothes for her finest, and walks out the town gate with her maid, straight into the enemy camp. She tells Holofernes she's come to help him win, and he is charmed.
On the fourth night he throws a banquet, drinks more than he ever has, and falls asleep. Alone in the tent, Judith takes his own sword and kills him.
She carries his head home in her food bag, and the leaderless army breaks and runs. It's a hard, bloody story, and the book doesn't look away.

It also doesn't read like a chronicle: it opens with Nabuchodonosor as king of the Assyrians, reigning in Nineveh, and some readers, Catholic scholars among them, take details like that as signs of a story told to teach.
What it teaches is clear: when the leaders gave up, a widow didn't.

how: Catholics hear Judith in the Liturgy of the Hours and at Mass, and the Church's liturgy applies the praise given to Judith, blessed above all women, to the Virgin Mary.

games.q: you're Judith. the elders have promised to surrender in five days if God doesn't act. what do you do?
o: wait the five days and see.
call the elders, rebuke them for testing God, and then act yourself.
slip out of the city and save yourself.
games.why: she calls them in: who are you to put God to the test? then she prays, and walks into the enemy camp.

practice: Think of a place you belong where the people in charge have quietly given up: a team, a parish committee, a family, a town that has set a deadline for hope.
Ask what one respectful, honest sentence you could say to them, the way Judith called the elders and told them the truth. If you pray, ask for her courage.

wordCard.voice: Judith. The widow of Bethulia who rebuked the elders for putting God on a deadline, and then went out and saved her city. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Judith, a Jewish woman, a woman of Judea. the book itself survives in Greek and Latin.

carryVoice: Your line: a widow saved the city. Faith that wouldn't set God a deadline. That's day four hundred thirty-nine.
